title: Is Calling Something 'The Big Lie' an Opinion?
hook: Defamation law protects opinion but not false facts — so the whole fight is over which side of that line a phrase falls on. Trump's suit against CNN asks the Supreme Court to redraw it.
key_points: Only false statements of fact can be defamatory; commentary and evaluation are protected speech.
Under Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. (1990), labeling something 'opinion' is not an automatic shield — what matters is whether it implies verifiable false facts.
Trump sued CNN over its use of 'the Big Lie' to describe his election claims, arguing the phrase equated him with Nazi propaganda.
A federal judge in Fort Lauderdale dismissed the case; the 11th Circuit affirmed, calling the phrase ambiguous rather than a false factual assertion.
His petition argues appeals courts are split between contextual multi-factor tests and more subjective assessments of when opinionated language conveys facts.
A cert petition is a request, not a ruling — CNN's response was due September 21, 2026.
content_html: Defamation law in the United States runs on a distinction that sounds simple and almost never is: you can be sued for stating a false fact about someone, but not for offering an opinion about them. President Trump's suit against CNN — over the network's use of "the Big Lie" to describe his claims about the 2020 election — is a clean illustration of how hard that line is to draw.
extra_html: As SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe reported, a federal judge in Fort Lauderdale dismissed the case and the 11th Circuit affirmed, reasoning that CNN never explicitly said Trump's conduct mirrored Hitler's and that "the Big Lie" was ambiguous rather than a false factual claim. Trump's petition for certiorari leans on Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. (1990), which held that a statement doesn't escape defamation law merely by wearing the label "opinion" — the question is whether it implies facts that can be proven false. He argues the appeals courts have splintered over how to run that test, some using contextual multi-factor analysis and others a more subjective read, and that the 11th Circuit brushed past the specific factual claims the phrase was shorthand for. Worth remembering what stage this is: asking the Supreme Court to hear a case is not winning it. CNN's response was due September 21, 2026, and the Court takes only a small fraction of petitions. (This card describes U.S. defamation law specifically.)

related.title: Freedom of Expression
related.hook: The freedom to speak, publish, and dissent is often called the first freedom — because without it, citizens can't check power or argue their way to better decisions.

related.title: The Free Press & Democracy
related.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

related.title: The Appeal After the Last Appeal
related.hook: When the Supreme Court declines your case, one option remains: ask it to reconsider. It has not granted such a request since 2018.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of statement can be defamatory, and what is protected?
flashcards.back_html: A false statement of fact can be defamatory. Commentary and evaluation — opinion — are protected speech.

flashcards.prompt: What did Milkovich v. Lorain Journal Co. (1990) establish?

choices.text: Calling a statement 'opinion' doesn't automatically shield it — courts ask whether it implies verifiable false facts
Any statement phrased as an opinion is absolutely immune from defamation suits
Public officials can never bring defamation claims

flashcards.explanation_html: The label doesn't decide it; whether the words convey checkable factual assertions does.

flashcards.prompt: Why did the 11th Circuit uphold dismissal of the CNN suit?

choices.text: It found 'the Big Lie' ambiguous rather than a false statement of fact
It held that news networks are exempt from defamation law
It ruled the case was filed after the deadline

flashcards.explanation_html: The court concluded CNN never explicitly claimed Trump's actions mirrored Hitler's, so the phrase wasn't a verifiable false fact.
